title: First — The Order That Decides the Outcome

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the nineteenth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three ahead. Gaza has a plan and a committee, and still nobody will move first.
The long bond went to a nineteen-year high — and did the Fed's job before the Fed did.
And a wok. [wry] The whole issue kept arguing about the same thing.
[amused] The order you do things in?
The order you do things in. Plato, on the cover: the beginning is the most important part of the work.
Okay. So — start with the beginning that's stuck. Gaza.
The whole deal is frozen on one word. First. The roadmap asks Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from about sixty per cent of Gaza it holds. Each side wants the other to go first.
And Netanyahu said no to the plan outright.
On the ninth. "Genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," first. So Washington sent Jared Kushner — Hamas in Cairo one day, Netanyahu in Jerusalem the next, about four hours.
[curious] And he got…?
Two working groups. One on disarmament, one on public health. And a line that it could all start in — quote — as little as thirty days.
[skeptical] Two working groups. That's not a withdrawal.
It is not. The sequencing gap that sank the plan is exactly where it was.
So how do we read it honestly? Because there's optimism in the room and nothing signed.
Read the dissent — it's cross-spectrum, which is the tell. On the right, Smotrich says Netanyahu is only halfway there. From the centre, Eisenkot is equally skeptical.
Same objection, opposite directions.

And there's an election on the twenty-seventh of October. Analysts read Netanyahu as chasing symbolic moves, not a real pull-back — because withdrawing three months before a vote is toxic. [pause] The committees might be the point. Motion without the move.
[sighs] Grim. What else moved on The World desk?

Fast, then. Ukraine ran one of the war's biggest deep-strike assaults — hundreds of drones into Russia, a warehouse near Moscow on fire. Russia hit back on the Odesa ports and a civilian ship on the Danube.
And the peace talks?
Unscheduled. Same shape as Gaza — nobody will front the first concession, so a strike stays cheaper than a first move.
Zambia — we held that one last week.

Called now. The commission declared President Hichilema re-elected, about sixty and a half per cent, a margin over a million votes. The loser rejected it, vowed a court challenge — and there was an armed raid on his home that's become the flashpoint.
Competing accounts.

Competing accounts. And keep two claims apart: the observers criticised the campaign; the opposition is disputing the count. A million-vote margin isn't the shape of a reversed tally. The honest verdict waits on the courts.
One more before we do money.
Flores. The earthquake off Indonesia — the toll's up to around sixty-eight, sixty-nine, and still climbing as they reach cut-off villages. About sixteen hundred aftershocks.
[thoughtful] Date the number and expect it to change.
Every time. A toll that rises isn't the wire getting it wrong. It's the wire getting it early.
[exhales] Okay. The money block. And you told me the bond market is the story this week — sorry, the point this week.

[wry] The point. The instrument that moved is the long bond. The US thirty-year printed about five point two nine per cent — a nineteen-year high. The ten-year near four point seven three. And the two-year fell.
Long end up, front end down. What's that called again?

A bear steepener. And it points somewhere specific — not "the Fed is too tight." The market's worry moved to the government that funds the deficit. July's federal shortfall was the largest since early twenty twenty-one, a recent thirty-year auction the priciest since two thousand and one.
So the long end repriced without waiting for the central bank.
It did the Fed's job first. Then it left the Fed to catch up. And the set-piece is next week — Jackson Hole, Friday the twenty-eighth, Kevin Warsh's first keynote as chair.
[curious] And a rate cut's still priced?
September, yes. But the long end is telling you the cut isn't the variable that matters — the term premium is. A dovish Warsh could steepen the curve further, not flatten it.
Give me the four-instrument read. What does it mean.

Regime is fiscal-fear-and-oil, equities held up only by the A-I bid. All-world equities sit near a record but rest on earnings, not easing. Global bonds face the worst backdrop — duration repriced by supply, not just the Fed.
And the two alternatives?

Gold is the standout — a record, around four thousand four hundred and twenty-nine an ounce, on fiscal fear and haven demand. Bitcoin is trading like a risk asset, not a hedge — choppy near sixty-four and a half thousand, lagging gold's bid.
Not advice, to be clear.
Explanation, not advice. And one honesty flag — a bond proxy we track is stale to early August, so we hold it rather than invent a fresh close.
Which lands us in Singapore, because the oil shock is the through-line.
It is. The Prime Minister gives the National Day Rally on Sunday. And the economy just got an upgrade — growth forecast raised to four and a half to five and a half per cent.
So it's a good-news speech.

[deadpan] It is not. The foreground is a power bill. Electricity and gas tariffs stepped up from July — an estimated twenty to thirty per cent, about thirty dollars a month more for a four-room flat. Pump prices up on the Middle-East shock.
And there's relief coming.

Vouchers. Four hundred to six hundred dollars to about two point four million citizens in September. But look at the order — the bill landed first, the cheque arrives after. A one-off payment against a permanent step-up in a recurring cost.
Relief that trails the bill.
That's the register Sunday gets heard in. Link your N-R-I-C to PayNow by the thirtieth of August to be paid earliest. And the July inflation print — we hold it. It's out around the twenty-fifth.
Good. Tech. Meta did something people didn't expect.
They opened a flagship again. Muse Glimmer — a thirty-billion-parameter model, multimodal, agentic, under an Apache two-point-oh licence. Download it, run it yourself.
[excited] After all the Llama licence fights. And the numbers?
Loud. Seventy-six on the SWE-bench coding test. But they're vendor-run, so treat them as reported, not settled — wait for the independent reruns.
Here's my question. Does it actually run at home? On his kind of rig?
That's the good part. Full precision is about sixty gigabytes, which wants sixty-four. So a two-card setup runs it native — no quantisation, no quality tax, room for the long context.
[warmly] So it just… fits.

It fits. The trade-off is speed — a dense model is slower per token than the sparse mixture-of-experts rivals. If you want throughput, they still win. If you want a capable agent that behaves the same way twice, this earns its memory.
And the export-control subplot rolls on.

The loophole nobody's closed — Chinese labs renting restricted compute offshore, which moves no hardware across a border, so it's lawful as written. The House voted three hundred and sixty-nine to twenty-two to close it. But it sits in the Senate, unvoted.
You can't ship the chip—
—but you can sell the hour. And the hour does the same work. A bill is not a rule.
[chuckles] Alright, a fast one for The Kit.
Google's Pixel eleven Pro Fold. Ships Thursday, nineteen hundred dollars — a hundred more than last year. Thinner, lighter, a back they call nearly impossible to crack.
So what's the catch? There's always a catch.
The battery got smaller. Down to four thousand eight hundred and six from over five thousand — while the price went up.
[skeptical] Nine grams thinner for ninety minutes less.
Engadget's line was "stagnating instead of innovating." The order-of-operations read: thinness you feel for a week, battery you feel for three years. Buy it for the screen, not the spec sheet.
And then — the maker of the day. The Atelier. This is woks, and I'm told the answer is: buy cheap.

[warmly] Buy cheap. It's a lovely conclusion. The metal does the cooking — carbon steel, rolled thin so it heats and responds in seconds. The whole spec is one line: fourteen inches, flat bottom, about two millimetres, long handle and a helper loop.
Skip nonstick, skip stainless.
Nonstick dies before it reaches the char. Stainless has no patina. And the non-stick surface you actually want, you make — you burn the pan blue and build a seasoning over years.
So the pan you keep is the pan you seasoned.
That's the buy-once case, made iron. A family wok, handed down darker and slicker than anything new. Rust is cosmetic — scrub, re-season, done.
[curious] But there's a grail tier. There's always a grail.

Hand-hammered. Thirty-six thousand hammer blows, the famous ones from Zhangqiu. And here's the sceptic — at home, a forty-five-dollar spun wok and a two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar hammered one, both seasoned on the same stove, cook the same food.
[laughs] So the hammering is a story.
Mostly a story. And after that documentary made Zhangqiu famous, counterfeits flooded in — machine-made pans stamped as hand-hammered. You can pay a hammered price for a machine pan.
And in Singapore?

Sia Huat, on Temple Street since nineteen fifty-nine — the trade's supplier. And a local truth: most flats run induction now, so buy flat-bottomed. The real wok hei belongs to the hawker's gas range. Spend the saved money on the heat, not the pan.
[amused] I love a desk that tells you to spend less. Okay. [drawn out] It's time, isn't it.
[deadpan] Don't.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week with this one. Fine. Indoor rowing. The erg.
[excited] The machine that never dies. Sell me on it.

It's the rare hobby where the entry purchase is the endgame purchase. A Concept Two rower — you buy it once, and race against it for the rest of your life. The hook is one number on a small screen: the split. Your pace per five hundred metres.
And the company's a bit of a legend.

Two brothers, nineteen seventy-six, Olympic hopefuls making oars out of the back of a bread truck in Vermont. Built the first indoor rower to keep the oar-makers busy through winter. Best-selling rower in the world ever since.
[curious] And they did something in twenty twenty-five?
Put the whole company into a perpetual-purpose trust — structured to stay independent forever. To a buy-once buyer, that reads as: not built to be sold or hollowed out.
So what does a new one cost?

Nine hundred and ninety US dollars for the standard model — about eighteen hundred and forty Singapore dollars. And the used market is a religion, because the machine doesn't die. Every wear part is cheap and you replace it yourself.
Okay, teach me the beginner mistake. Because there's always one.
The damper. People crank it to ten thinking harder is better. It just loads the stroke, wrecks your grip and your lower back, and gasses you early. It's called rowing in mud.
[amused] Rowing in mud.
The elites sit at three to five. And you don't set resistance by the lever — you set it by the drag factor, the real number the monitor reads. Aim a hundred and ten to a hundred and thirty.
And the stroke itself — there's an order to that too, isn't there.
[warmly] Of course there is. Drive: legs, then body, then arms. Recovery: arms, body, legs — reversed. Get the order wrong and the back pays. It's the whole issue in one movement.
And the ritual? The thing everyone measures?
The two-thousand-metre test. One rower calls it the S-A-T of rowing. Everyone knows their time. And there's a million-metre club — people row, quite literally, for the certificate.
[laughs] Okay but you have to give me the sceptic. This thing lives in a lot of spare rooms.
[wry] The most abandoned machine in the house. The classic clothes rack. Even happy owners admit units gathering dust.
So why's it still the buy-once pick?

Resale. Unlike a budget rower nobody will buy back, a used Concept Two returns most of your money. So a failed habit is a cheap mistake. And the deeper caution — the two-k is a test, not a workout. Row only all-out and you're just hurting, not training.
[warmly] Learn the order first. Chase the number last.
That's the whole hobby. [pause] Alright — come back up. Culture and the body, quickly.
Music first. There's a record everyone's raving about.
L'Rain — "fata morgana." Eighty-two at Pitchfork, album of the week at Stereogum. A collage — dancehall, gospel, crunched metal, all in half an hour.
[curious] But you had a caveat.

The admired-versus-replayed question. It's dense, unresolved, headphone music. More likely to be admired than reached for. A critics' album and a daily-driver album are different objects — and this is the first.
[amused] The score measures the critic, not your Tuesday commute.
Exactly that. Good Life — a watch. TAG Heuer, a Formula One in Zandvoort orange, for the final Dutch Grand Prix. Solar quartz — a minute of sun buys about a day, a full charge runs ten months.
That's genuinely practical. Price?

Two thousand one hundred and fifty US dollars, fifteen hundred pieces. But — sceptic — the grey market was already listing it around two thousand three-fifty to two thousand five-seventy before buyers even had it.
[chuckles] So "limited" is doing some acting.
Buy it to wear, not to flip. Family desk — and this one's the spine again. The biggest school phone-ban study yet.
[curious] And the verdict?
Well-being went up — more than switching off Facebook, in one comparison. But here's the order. In year one, discipline got worse and well-being dipped. The payoff only showed up by year three.
[thoughtful] So the families who quit in year one never reach the year that pays.
That's the finding. And on grades? Close to zero. So the case isn't "it lifts results." It's "it helps the climate, slowly, if you hold the line."
And the don't-be-alarmist note, because you promised one.

Candice Odgers argues the "phones cause a crisis" claim outruns the data — that moral panic distracts from real drivers. The honest read: modest, contested associations, strongest in early-adolescent girls. Not a proven switch. Calm beats crisis.
There was a sleep finding too.

A good one for an eleven-year-old. The later bedtimes track puberty, not age — it's biology, not defiance. But a set bedtime still works: about twenty minutes more sleep a night. The lever survives the hormones.
And fitness — the barbell before the protein.

[warmly] The cleanest one all issue. Whey plus lifting builds lean mass. But a clean trial found leucine — the supplement everyone sprinkles — did nothing to preserve muscle without the training. The barbell builds it; the powder is just raw material.
Order again. Stimulus first.
Aim about one point six grams of protein per kilo, twenty-five to thirty a meal. But two or three lifting sessions a week is the ingredient you can't skip.
[amused] And the Diary — because October's a problem.

October's booked solid. The Weeknd's two Singapore nights collide with the Formula One Sprint weekend, so reserve dining now, tickets after. And on the table — Assaggi, on Neil Road, from the chef behind one-Michelin Buona Terra. Set menus, eighty-eight dollars for the tasting.
Worth it?
Promising — but under two weeks old, so it's first impressions, not a verdict. And a fish grill finally opened, Shinpachi, teishoku from eight dollars ninety. Cheap, and easy with a kid.
[warmly] Okay. Bring us down. The Undercurrent.

[drawn out] This one's quieter. The Philippines. For a decade, the social-media capital of the world — the country where Facebook basically became the internet, and where that hollowed out trust in the news.
And now?

Now, quietly, young Filipinos are drifting to Reddit. Anonymous, text-first, community-run — the near-exact opposite of the feed they grew up in. Reddit's reach jumped about two hundred and fifty per cent last year.
[thoughtful] And the trust?
Fell to twenty-eight per cent, down ten points in a year — the steepest fall of forty-eight countries studied. The refuge and the collapse are the same event, read from two sides.
So which came first?

[drawn out] The trust collapsed first. Over years. The migration is the delayed effect — because people don't leave a public square while they still believe in it. The two-thousand-tens promised real names would civilise the web. They're voting the other way now — that you can only speak honestly when nobody can attach it to your face.
[thoughtful] And the honest caveat?

DataReportal itself warns the reach jump might be a reporting artifact, not real users. And Facebook still reaches ninety-seven per cent of them. So it's a tremor, not a tide. But the magnitude's contestable — the direction isn't. The country that ran the experiment furthest is the first to read the result.
[warmly] The beginning is the most important part of the work.
And the beginning here was the loss of trust — years ago, in a feed built to reward the opposite of it. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
